case_name: Steele v. Riverside Forest Products et al. and Raboch v. Riverside Forest Products et al.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF
BRITISH
COLUMBIA

Citation:

Steele v.
Riverside Forest
Products
et al. and Raboch v.
Riverside

Forest
Products et al. ,

2005 BCSC 1598

Date: 20051117

Docket:
S051179

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Gordon Steele

Plaintiff

And

Riverside Forest Products Limited,
Tolko Industries Ltd.

And James Allan Thorlakson

Defendants

Docket:
S051180

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Gerald Raboch

Plaintiff

And

Riverside Forest Products Limited,
Tolko Industries Ltd.

And James Alan Thorlakson

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Master A.N. Patterson

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiffs

B.M.
Greyall

Counsel for the Defendants

S.M.
Mitchell

Date and Place of Hearing:

October
25, 2005

Vancouver, B.C.

[
1
]

The defendant Thorlakson applies in both actions
for an order that he is not a proper party to the actions or alternatively for
an order that portions of the statements of claim containing references to him
be struck out.  The result of either application being successful would be the
actions being dismissed as against him.

[
2
]

The actions are brought by the former chief
executive officer and the former chief financial officer of the defendant
Riverside Forest Products Limited (hereinafter Riverside) who allege that they
were wrongfully dismissed and they claim payment of certain retirement benefits
and damages.

[
3
]

The actions arise out of a hostile takeover of
the defendant Riverside by the
defendant Tolko Industries Ltd. (hereinafter Tolko) in 2004 when the defendant
Tolko acquired nearly all of the issued shares of the defendant Riverside.  Subsequent to the takeover, the
plaintiffs were dismissed.

[
4
]

The pleadings in the two actions are virtually
identical, in each case there has been a statement of claim, a statement of
defence and counterclaim, a statement of defence to the counterclaims and a
reply.

[
5
]

The defendant Thorlakson relies on Supreme Court
Rules 15(5) and 19(24) which are as follows:

Rule 15

(5)(a)   At
any stage of a proceeding, the court on application by any person may

1.         order that a party, who is not or has ceased to be a
proper or necessary party, cease to be a party,

Rule 19

(24)     At
any stage of a proceeding the court may order to be struck out or amended the
whole or any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the
ground that

(a)       it discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case
may be,

(b)       it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)       it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may
grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order
the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
6
]

The principles to be applied on applications
pursuant to Rule 19(24) have been conveniently summarized by Romilly J. in
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J.
No. 2160 (S.C.) as follows:

To succeed on an application under Rule
19(24)(a) it must be established that it is “plain and obvious” that the
pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:  Hunt v. Carey Canada,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990]
2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.).  If there is any doubt it should be resolved in favour
of permitting the pleadings to stand:  McGauley v. British
Columbia (1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223 (B.C.C.A.).  The
court should proceed on the assumption that all the facts pled are true:
Helman v. Brown (1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C.C.A.).  The only question then is
whether the facts disclose a cause of action:  Minnes v. Minnes (1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39
W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.); McNauthton v. Baker (1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (C.A.).  In other words, as long as the
pleadings disclose a triable issue, either as it exists, or as it may be
amended, then the issue should go to trial.  The mere fact that the case is
weak or not likely to succeed is no ground for striking it out under the
provisions of Rule 19(24):  Minnes, supra.

[
7
]

That statement by Romilly J. has been approved
by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in
Porier v. Community Futures
Development Corp. of Mt. Waddington

[2005] B.C.J. No.763 (C.A.) (Q.L.)
169
paragraph 9.

[
8
]

By analogy a similar criteria would apply to an
application pursuant to Rule 15(5) in determining whether a party has ceased to
be a proper or necessary party to the proceedings.

[
9
]

The statements of claim make the following
references to the defendant Thorlakson after identifying him as the president
and chief executive officer of the defendant Tolko in paragraph 6:

17.       Riverside, acting on the instructions of Tolko and/or Thorlakson, or on its
own behalf, refused to pay the Vacation Pay to the Plaintiff, although various
requests were made in that regard.  Riverside finally paid the Vacation Pay to the Plaintiff, less statutory
deductions, on or about January 31, 2005, three months after termination.

18.       Riverside, acting on the instructions of Tolko and/or Thorlakson, or on its
own behalf, has refused to pay the Plaintiff pay in lieu of reasonable notice
although expressly requested to do so on a number of occasions.  The
termination of the Plaintiff’s employment with Riverside constitutes a wrongful dismissal.

19.       Furthermore, Riverside, acting on the instructions of Tolko and/or Thorlakson, or on its
own behalf, has refused to pay the Plaintiff the Lump Sum Payment that is due
and owing under the RAA, although requested to do so on a number of occasions.
Riverside finally paid a
portion of the Lump sum Payment to the Plaintiff on or about January 25, 2005
in the amount of approximately $3,050,000.

20.       In addition, Riverside, acting on the instructions of Tolko and/or Thorlakson, or on its
own behalf, refused to pay the Plaintiff benefits pursuant to the Defined
Benefit Pension Plan, although requested to do so on a number of occasions.  Riverside finally paid the Plaintiff these
benefits on or about February 14, 2005.

21.       The conduct of the Defendants as
described in paragraphs 17, 18, 19 and 20 herein, constitutes bad faith conduct
in the manner in which the Plaintiff was terminated, warranting increased
damages for wrongful dismissal.

22.       Tolko and Thorlakson participated in Riverside’s wrongful conduct by directing,
or otherwise causing, Riverside’s
Board of Directors to act in the manner described herein, including but not
limited to, wrongfully interfering with the contractual relations between the
Plaintiff and Riverside.  The
Plaintiff claims damages for inducing breach of contract against Tolko and
Thorlakson, who with the knowledge of the employment contract between Riverside
and the Plaintiff, the RAA and the Defined Benefit Pension Plan, and with the
intent to prevent the performance of said contracts, wrongfully procured and
induced Riverside to breach its contracts with the Plaintiff.  By reason of
these acts the Plaintiff has suffered damages.

. . .

26.       The Plaintiff claims aggravated and
punitive damages against the Defendants, the particulars of which the Plaintiff
relies on in support of this claim include those described in paragraphs 17,
18, 19, 20 and 22 herein.

[
10
]

It is to be noted that in paragraphs 17 to 20
the pleadings are framed as “Riverside” acting on the instructions of “Tolko and/or Thorlakson.”  The
defendant Tolko is, of course, by this time the majority shareholder of the
defendant Riverside and the
defendant Thorlakson is President and Chief Executive Officer of the defendants
Riverside and Tolko.  There is
no pleading specific to the defendant Thorlakson in his personal capacity.

[
11
]

In paragraph 21 the plaintiff pleads that the
allegations in paragraphs 17 to 20 constitute bad faith.  Again, there is no
specific pleading of bad faith on the part of the defendant Thorlakson.

[
12
]

In paragraph 22 there is, in effect, a pleading
that the defendant Thorlakson and the defendant Tolko interfered with the
plaintiff’s contractual relations with the defendant Riverside or induced the defendant Riverside to breach its contract with the plaintiffs.

[
13
]

The defendants have filed statements of defence
and counterclaims in which the plaintiffs’ claims are denied and they contain
the following paragraphs:

19.       In further answer to paragraph 22 of
the Statement of Claim, on or about November 1, 2004, Thorlakson because a
director, as well as the President and Chief Executive Officer of Riverside.

20.       In further answer to paragraph 22 of
the Statement of Claim, in all dealings with the Plaintiff, Thorlakson was
acting
bona fide
in the scope of his duties as director, President, and
Chief Executive Officer of Tolko, and then as director, President and Chief
Executive Officer of Riverside, and not out of any personal interest, fraud or
malice, but in the best interests of Tolko and Riverside.

[
14
]

In my view, it makes no difference that the
defendant Thorlakson has, with the other defendants, delivered a statement of
defence as both rules relied upon in these applications provide that the
applications can be made “at any stage of a proceeding.”

[
15
]

The defendant Thorlakson relies upon a principle
initially stated in
Said v. Butt

[1920] 3 K.B. 497
.  In that
case, a theatre patron sued the defendant who was managing director of a
theatre company.  McCardie J. gave a considered judgment and held that a
servant of a company acting
bona fide
within the scope of his authority
causing or procuring a breach of contract does not thereby become personally
liable for the tort of inducing breach of contract.

[
16
]

That principle has been relied upon on numerous
occasions in this court.  In
Dorus v. Tech Corp.
(2002) B.C.C.A.
241 the court refused leave to appeal an order of Gill J. dismissing the
plaintiff’s case against the personal defendants who were officers and employees
of the defendant companies pursuant to Rule 19(24).  In that case Gill J.
wrote:

[19]      When the matter first came on for
hearing on May 8, 2001, Mr. Dorus seemed to acknowledge that officers or
directors of companies could not be liable simply because they were the
directing minds of a company.  In that regard, I refer to Normart Management
Ltd. v. Westhill Redevelopment Co. (1998),
1998 CanLII 2447 (ON CA)
, 37 O.R. (3d) 97 (C.A.) where it was
noted that an agreement between two companies to injure can amount to the tort
of conspiracy but that does not mean that the directing minds are themselves
parties to the conspiracy and it is not sufficient to merely assert that these
individuals conspired to injure.  Further, as has been stated in many
authorities, in order to establish a cause of action against an employee or
director of a corporation, a plaintiff must show that the individual committed
a tortuous act which demonstrated an identity or interest separate from that of
the company:  see Lasik Vision Canada Inc. v. T.L.C. Vancouver Optimetric Group
Inc.,
1999 CanLII 1002 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No.2796, December 7, 1999, Vancouver Registry No. C981969
(S.C.), at para.24.

[
17
]

In
Digital Document Service v. Future Shop
Ltd. et al.
Vancouver
Registry No. C965918, Warren J. in reasons for judgment dated June 19, 1997, on an application to strike out
the claims against individual defendants who were officers of the defendant
Future Shop pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 19(24) allowed that application and
said this:

[18]      On the materials before me, I am
satisfied that all of the allegations made by the plaintiffs against the
individual defendants focus on their conduct as agents of the corporate
defendant and they were acting within the ordinary course and scope of their
employment responsibilities.  There is no allegation that any of the individual
defendants acted for personal gain or out of malice toward the plaintiffs.  In
my view, the plaintiffs’ claims against the personal defendants disclose no
reasonable cause of action and the claims are bound to fail.  (See Craik v.
Aetna Life Insurance Co. of Canada
[1995] O.J. No. 3286
, November 1, 1995.)

[
18
]

In reaching that decision Warren J. relied upon
the principle that an agent is not liable for inducing a breach of contract
while acting in good faith and for the protection of his employer’s interests.

[
19
]

In
Glenayre Manufacturing Ltd. v. Pilot
Pacific Properties Inc.

2003 BCSC 303
(leave to appeal denied) Melnick
J. considered the correct test in determining whether officers or employees of
a limited company could be separately liable.  Melnick J. concluded that a
director or officer is protected from liability unless their actions are
themselves tortious or exhibit a separate identity or interest from that of the
company so as to make the act complained about their own.

[
20
]

In coming to  a decision on an application of
this nature the court must assume the facts that have been pleaded are factual
and that they disclose no triable issue as they now exist or as they may
amended.  Referring to the statements of claim, it is clear from paragraphs 17
to 20 that the defendant Riverside, on instructions from its majority shareholder and its chief
executive officer, acted or failed to act on the plaintiffs’ requests.  There
is nothing in those paragraphs which indicates that Thorlakson was acting in
any way outside the scope of his authority.  Further, the pleadings do not
disclose any activity on the part of Thorlakson with an identity or interest separate
from that of the company.  No separate tort is pleaded.

[
21
]

Paragraph 21 of the statement of claim adds nothing
to what has already been pleaded.  There are no particulars of bad faith
alleged on the part of the defendant Thorlakson.  As noted earlier, all of the
allegations are pleaded as “Riverside acting on the instructions of the
defendant Tolko and/or the defendant Thorlakson” clearly showing that the
plaintiff viewed those acts as the actions of the defendant Riverside alone.

[
22
]

Paragraph 22 contains the pleading of inducing
breach of contract which has been specifically dealt with in the cases.  There
is no pleading that the defendant Thorlakson acted maliciously, without
authority or was engaged in fraud, deceit or dishonesty.

[
23
]

In my view, no independent cause of action has
been pleaded except for those covered by the decision in
Said v. Butt
,
consequently,  the plaintiffs’ actions as against the defendant Thorlakson are
bound to fail and no amendment can save them.  It follows that the claims
against the defendant Thorlakson are struck out, the actions against him are dismissed
and he is no longer a proper party to either action.

[
24
]

In the circumstances the defendant Thorlakson is
entitled to his costs in each action on Scale 3.

“Master
A.N. Patterson”
